findings.title: Early return on `dateOverrideExist` bypasses all busy-time checks
findings.body: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, if a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls within the override's time window, lines 133-135 immediately `return true` before reaching the `busy.every(...)` loop at line 153. As a result, any existing bookings or external calendar busy events on a day with a date override are completely ignored, allowing already-booked slots to be shown as available and double-booked.

findings.title: Dayjs object reference comparison and boundary checks in date override validation are broken
findings.body:
Inside the `dateOverrides.find` callback in `checkIfIsAvailable`:
1. Line 114 compares two fresh Dayjs instances with `===` (`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`), which compares object references and is always `false`. An all-day 'unavailable' date override (where `start` and `end` are equal) is therefore never detected as Equal, and if a slot happens to match that timestamp it won't be rejected.
2. Lines 118-125 reject a slot only when `slotEndTime <= overrideStart` or `slotStartTime > overrideEnd` (i.e. completely disjoint from the override), rather than when `slotStartTime < overrideStart || slotEndTime > overrideEnd`. Slots that only partially overlap the date override window, or that start at `overrideEnd`, are treated as valid.
3. Using `.find()` means that if a user has multiple date override ranges on the same day, the first range that does not contain the slot causes `find` to return truthy and the whole check to return `false`, even if the slot falls inside a second override range on that day.

findings.title: Working hours check in `checkIfIsAvailable` uses `slotStartTime` for `end` and rejects valid split schedules
findings.body:
In `checkIfIsAvailable` (lines 138-151):
1. Line 142 computes `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` instead of using `slotEndTime`, so it never verifies that the end of the slot fits within `workingHour.endTime`.
2. Because it uses `workingHours.find(...)` to look for a violated entry rather than checking whether *some* working-hour interval contains the slot (`!workingHours.some(...)`), any user with multiple working-hour blocks on the same day (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 13:00-17:00) will have every slot rejected: a morning slot fails the afternoon block's `start < workingHour.startTime` check, and an afternoon slot fails the morning block's `end > workingHour.endTime` check.
3. If a user has no working hours at all on `slotStartTime.day()`, `find` returns `undefined` and the function treats the user as available on their day off.

findings.title: `dateOverrides` already have organizer UTC offset applied, causing double offset or day-wrap errors in `getSlots`
findings.body: `getUserAvailability` already shifts each `dateOverride.start` and `end` by the organizer's UTC offset when constructing `dateOverrides`. In `getSlots` (lines 212-224), `override.start` is shifted again by `inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset` instead of just `inviteeUtcOffset`, and `startTime`/`endTime` are computed with `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` after adding the offset. When the timezone offset pushes `override.end` to `00:00` of the next day (or `override.start` into the previous day), `.hour() * 60 + .minute()` wraps around to `0` (or a large value from the previous day), producing an invalid range (`startTime >= endTime`) and dropping all slots for that override.
